sections.body:
Information overload is the state in which the amount of information coming at you exceeds the amount you can process. It is not simply "a lot of news". It is the point where each new piece of information makes the others harder to use, because your attention, your memory and your judgment all have fixed budgets.

The human brain is a superb pattern finder but a slow serial processor. It can hold only a handful of ideas at once. When the feed never ends, the brain adapts in the cheapest way it can: it skims. Skimming feels like reading, but it leaves almost nothing behind.

Researchers call the result the **paradox of choice applied to knowledge**: the more options and facts you face, the less satisfied you are with any of them, and the less deeply any of them is understood.
examples: You open your phone to check one message and twenty minutes later you have read forty headlines, none of which you can repeat.
sections.heading: What information overload actually is

sections.body:
There is an old distinction between two kinds of knowledge. **Knowing that** something is true — a fact, a headline, a statistic — and **knowing how** an idea hangs together, where it comes from, and what it implies. Information overload floods the first kind while starving the second.

A person can know hundreds of true facts about the economy, the climate or the human body and still be unable to explain how any of them work. Each fact arrived with no time to connect it to the others, so the facts sit in memory like loose change in a drawer.

Understanding is a structural thing. It lives in the connections between facts, not in the facts themselves. When the input never pauses, the connections never form. That is why a day of heavy reading can end with the strange feeling of having learned nothing at all.
examples: You have read twenty articles about inflation, but you still cannot explain to a friend why prices at the market went up.
sections.heading: Knowing about is not the same as knowing

sections.body:
Information is produced because attention can be sold. Every article, video and notification competes for a fixed budget of human attention, and the competition has shaped the information itself. Loud beats quiet. Certain beats uncertain. New beats important.

The result is a daily diet of content optimized for the eye rather than the mind. The information that survives this selection is not the information you would have chosen for yourself. It is the information that was best at grabbing you.

Recognizing this changes the question. The question is no longer "how do I keep up with everything?" — nobody keeps up — but "who chose what I read today, and would I have chosen it myself?"
examples: A calm, careful explanation of how vaccines work will almost always lose to a shocking story about one rare side effect.
sections.heading: The economics of attention

sections.body: A small set of terms describes the mechanics of overload. They are worth learning precisely, because each one names a force you will meet again tomorrow.
sections.heading: The vocabulary of overload

terms.example: After an hour of headlines, I stopped reading carefully; that is information overload at work.
terms.gloss: The state in which incoming information exceeds the capacity to process it, so each new item reduces the value of the ones before it.

terms.example: Taking notes by hand lowers my cognitive load, because I process each idea as I write it.
terms.gloss: The total amount of mental effort being used by working memory at one time.

terms.example: In the attention economy, a notification is a product feature designed to pull you back into an app.
terms.gloss: The market in which businesses compete for people's limited attention and resell it to advertisers.

terms.example: My group chat has a terrible signal-to-noise ratio: three hundred messages to learn one fact.
terms.gloss: The proportion of useful information (signal) to everything else (noise) in a stream of content.

terms.example: He has shallow knowledge of five programming languages and cannot write one complete program.
terms.gloss: Familiarity with the surface of many topics without understanding of how any of them works.

terms.example: She knew the storm had passed, but she kept doomscrolling through the damage reports until two in the morning.
terms.gloss: The habit of continuously consuming negative news, especially in a feed, long past the point of usefulness.

sections.body: Feeds are built on variable rewards: the next item might be amazing, so the brain keeps pulling the lever. This is the same mechanism as a slot machine. The discomfort you feel when you stop is not a sign that you need more information — it is a sign that the mechanism worked on you.
sections.heading: Why your brain keeps scrolling

sections.body:
You cannot read everything, so the only real strategy is to choose earlier and forgive yourself sooner. A workable filter has three questions. First: **Will I act on this?** If no information can change any decision you will make, the article is entertainment, and it should admit it. Second: **Is this the best source on this topic I know?** One good explanation beats twenty hot takes. Third: **Have I finished the last thing I started?** Unfinished reading is a debt that makes new reading shallower.

Many heavy readers keep a short "later" list. The list is not a prison — it is a promise that the article is safely stored, which lowers the fear of missing out that drives compulsive reading. Most items on the list can be deleted a week later with no loss at all.
examples: Before saving an article, ask: what will I do differently after reading this?
sections.heading: A practical filter for the daily flood

sections.body:
The opposite of overload is not ignorance. It is a small, well-kept garden of things you understand. Readers who keep their knowledge for years tend to share three habits.

They **finish**. One article read to the end, with notes, teaches more than ten articles skimmed. They **revisit**. Understanding fades on a predictable schedule, and a ten-minute review after a week, a month and a year beats any marathon session. And they **explain**. Teaching an idea to another person is the fastest test of whether you own it or have merely rented it.

Information overload ends the moment you decide that your mind is not a warehouse for facts but a workshop for a few ideas you are slowly getting right.
examples: She reads one long essay every Sunday and writes a half-page summary in her own words. A year later she can still explain every one of them.
sections.heading: From collecting information to keeping knowledge

item.summary: The average person meets more information in a day than a medieval farmer met in a year. This article explains what information overload does to understanding, why more facts can produce less knowledge, and how to turn an endless feed into a small set of things you actually know.
item.title: Information Overload: When Knowing Too Much Means Understanding Too Little
